transcript.text: I lead retention at a subscription company. I want a model that tells us, for each customer, which discount to offer (none, 10 percent or 25 percent) so that they do not leave. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. We have never given discounts before, so there is no record of any offer or of how customers reacted. The retention team would use the result every month. [shares customers.csv]

I'll look at the table before saying anything about what it can support.

Your table supports half of what you asked for — I want to be precise about which half before we pick a route.

Here's the honest read before you pick. Your table can tell you **who is about to leave**. It cannot tell you **which discount keeps them**. Across all 1,200 customers churn runs 17.4%, and the signal is real: basic 22.4% versus plus 11.1%, consumer 18.1% versus business 14.6%, and the 388 customers with 2 or more support tickets in the last 90 days churn at 20.1%. I checked for leakage and found no column written after the outcome, so a risk model on these fields is clean. But a "which discount" model is a causal question, and answering it needs customers who *were* offered something and customers who weren't. You've never given discounts, so that variation doesn't exist in any data you own — no algorithm can conjure it. If we trained on this table today and called the output a discount recommendation, it would just be a churn score wearing a label, and the retention team would be spending margin on people who were never going to leave. So my suggestion is to run the two tracks side by side: score risk now so the month isn't wasted, and start collecting offer response deliberately so the real model becomes possible in a few months. The options below cover that — a risk model with the discount depth set by your policy, the design of the small randomized test that makes a response model trainable, and a monthly retention read to hold the team while those are built. One thing I'd need either way: roughly what share of customers you can actually afford to discount each month, and whether any plan is off-limits (premium margins, for instance). Which of these do you want to start with?

choices.title: Risk model now, discount depth by policy
choices.what: Train a churn model on the 1200 rows you have (plan, segment, tenure, spend, tickets, signup date) and score every customer each month into risk tiers; you then set the discount rule yourself (e.g. top-risk tier gets 25%, next tier 10%, the rest none). You get: A working monthly per-customer risk score with measured accuracy on a holdout, plus a simple tier-to-discount table the retention team can run this month. Trade-off: It says who is likely to leave, not what a discount does for them. Any tier-to-discount mapping is your judgement, not learned evidence, so some customers will be discounted who would have stayed anyway. Effort: 1 build now, retrained as new months land.

choices.title: Design the discount test that makes the model possible
choices.what: A written pilot plan: offer none / 10% / 25% at random inside the high-risk group, sized from your real churn rates (11.1% on plus, 22.4% on basic) so it can detect a difference, with the guardrails and the data fields to record so a response model is trainable afterwards. You get: Sample sizes, allocation, stop rules and the logging schema; after 2-3 months of it you have the offer-and-reaction history that a true which-discount model needs. Trade-off: No new prediction this month, and it costs a slice of the discount budget on customers picked by chance rather than by need. Effort: One brief today; 2-3 months of running the pilot.

choices.title: Monthly retention read first
choices.what: A dashboard kept in this chat: churn by plan, segment, tenure band and ticket level, refreshed on request each month. You get: The retention team sees where churn actually sits before anyone spends a discount, and the numbers to set the pilot's guardrails. Trade-off: Descriptive only; no per-customer score, so outreach still runs on human judgement. Effort: Quick, and it stays live to refresh.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a travel agency. I want to predict, at the moment a booking is made, whether it will be cancelled, so the operations team can overbook the right trips. The table I shared is our bookings up to late February 2026: booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Some of the trips in it have not happened yet. Operations would score every new booking once, on the day it is made. [shares bookings.csv]

I read your table before proposing anything — here's what it says. 1,500 bookings, 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-24 booking dates, 343 cancelled: a 22.9% base rate, no missing labels, and it holds fairly steady month to month (19.5% to 27.8%). Real separable signal exists: cancelled bookings sit on longer lead times (mean 103.6 days vs 87.22 for kept ones), and destinations spread from 18.9% (Paris) to 26.2% (Dubai). Channels barely differ (22.6% to 23.8%), and free_cancellation looks almost inert (22.6% vs 23.3%) — worth checking that field is populated as you think. Three housekeeping things matter for a clean test: price holds 1,126 distinct values read as text (needs converting to numeric), 12 rows carry destination "TEST", and 865 distinct customer_id across 1,500 bookings means repeat travellers — so the split has to be by customer, or the same person leaks across train and test. The trap I want to flag: 318 bookings have travel dates still ahead (up to 2026-08-16). Their "not cancelled" is really "not cancelled *yet*". Since operations scores a booking once, on its booking day, the honest test is a time-based holdout on bookings whose cancellation window has actually closed — that's exactly the situation your model will face in production. Random splits would flatter the model. Three ways forward below. My recommendation: the model, built with the time-based holdout and censoring rule stated up front — then the overbooking economics to turn probabilities into seats.

choices.title: Cancellation-risk model at booking time
choices.what: Train a classifier on cancelled using only what is known the moment the booking is made (destination, nationality, channel, lead_time_days, price, free_cancellation, plus travel_date-derived seasonality). Time-based holdout: train on early bookings, test on the latest months, split by customer_id so repeat travellers don't leak; drop the 12 destination='TEST' rows, convert price to numeric, and exclude bookings whose cancellation window has not closed yet. You get: A calibrated probability per new booking plus a lift table (cancellation rate by risk decile out of holdout) that operations can turn into a threshold, and a read of which features actually move the risk. Trade-off: With 1,500 rows and a 22.9% base rate, expect a modest lift over 22.9%, not a sharp分离器; the honest test is holdout lift, not accuracy. Effort: One build, holdout metrics and charts back in this chat.

choices.title: Risk map of your trips first, no model
choices.what: Slice cancellation by destination, lead-time band, travel month, nationality and channel over the bookings whose travel date has passed, and show which segments carry the most cancellable seats. You get: A report and dashboard operations can use today to set overbooking per segment, and a clear view of how much separable signal exists before any model is built. Trade-off: Segment averages only: they say nothing about an individual booking, and thin segments are noisy. Effort: Fast, queries in this turn.

choices.title: Turn a score into seats: overbooking rule
choices.what: A brief that works out, per departure size, how many extra seats to sell from a given cancellation probability, comparing the cost of an empty seat with bumping a passenger, including the risk of concentrating overbooked seats on one departure. You get: The decision rule and its money maths, plus the threshold a score should be cut at; this is what makes the model useful rather than just accurate. Trade-off: Needs your per-seat and bumping costs; without them the numbers stay illustrative. Effort: Short write-up, no model.

- **Label rule:** the 318 bookings with travel dates still ahead are excluded from training and testing — their "not cancelled yet" would teach the model the wrong lesson. - **Split:** by time on booking_date (train on earlier months, test on the most recent), and by customer_id, so a repeat traveller can't appear on both sides. - **Outcome column:** `cancelled`. Leakage check came back clean — no column in the table looks like it's written after the cancellation happens, so every field you listed is legitimately known at booking time. One thing I'll need from you after results, to set the operating threshold: what an empty seat costs versus bumping a passenger on a trip. That's the overbooking maths, not the model — no need to answer now. Want me to have DCLab build it now?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

The build is running now — DCLab is checking the remaining requirements, so no numbers yet. Two things my pre-build review turned up that shape what you'll get:

- `booking_id` is not unique: 12 rows share an id but differ in travel date, price or outcome, so it's a weak identifier, not a row key. I'm keeping all 1,500 rows rather than dropping them, and the split will group on `customer_id`. The model will lean on it heavily. I've asked whether that's a genuine market effect or a proxy for which trips you sell — I'll tell you which way it falls once the model's feature importance is out. Two smaller notes I've logged for after results: the recent slice is a last-minute-cancellation tail (short lead times cancelling at far higher rates than long ones), so the cancellation window genuinely closes at the booking date rather than the travel date; and `cancelled` is the only flag-shaped column with no missing values, so a field that isn't populated cleanly is a label issue, not a feature.
